## The problem

A retail marketing team had committed to a content strategy that its production capacity could not sustain. Video content was needed across more than eighteen digital touchpoints, each with its own format specification — and all of it was produced manually by a single in-house designer.

The question was not simply whether AI could generate video. It was whether AI could take on the repetitive work without compromising a brand the company had spent decades building.

::: {.callout-note}
## My role
Six-person consultancy team. I owned the **systematic literature review** and the **synthesis of combined research findings** — the two chapters that connect published evidence to the design decisions in the build.
:::

## Approach

The project followed **Design Science Research** (Hevner et al., 2004), which is designed for work whose output is a built artefact rather than an explanation. Four evidence streams fed the design:

| Stream | What it established |
|--------|--------------------|
| Systematic literature review | What these architectures can reliably do today |
| Semi-structured interviews | What stakeholders actually needed |
| Process mapping (BPMN 2.0) | Where time is lost in the current workflow |
| Requirements traceability matrix | Which feature satisfies which requirement |

No design decision rested on a single source. Eight decisions were documented, each cross-checked against all four streams before it entered the build.

## The literature review

I ran the review following **Okoli's eight-step procedure**, with **PRISMA 2020** governing the search and screening, and **systematic mapping** (Petersen et al., 2008) as the synthesis method.

The search combined two keyword clusters — one for architectures (RAG, LLMs, transformer models, diffusion), one for the content-creation task (text-to-video, automated editing) — requiring a match from each, so that a transformer paper without a content application would not return.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["1,799 records<br/>identified"] --> B["159 full texts<br/>sought"]
    B --> C["154 assessed<br/>against 3 criteria"]
    C --> D["45 studies<br/>included"]
```

Three eligibility criteria had to pass: a technically grounded architecture described in detail, video or multimodal output demonstrated experimentally, and evidence of real-world applicability. Every exclusion was recorded against the criterion it failed, so the selection is transparent and repeatable.

Each included study was then characterised against six predefined attributes using a shared codebook, producing the taxonomy the design decisions were drawn from.

### What the review found

**Compound pipelines are the state of the art.** Twenty-seven of the forty-five studies chain specialised components across planning, generation and quality control rather than relying on a single model. This directly shaped the eight-stage architecture.

**No single technique holds a brand.** The literature identifies four control mechanisms — LoRA fine-tuning, ControlNet spatial conditioning, IP-Adapter reference injection, and retrieval from a curated library — and finds that they have to be layered. Prompt conditioning alone is explicitly flagged as insufficient.

**Governance is the least studied part of the field.** Human oversight appeared in only ten of the forty-five studies, and almost always as a secondary concern rather than the contribution being made.

That last finding was the one that shaped the design most. Every stakeholder interviewed described human approval as non-negotiable — so the part the client cared about most was the part the literature had least to say about.

## What we built

An eight-stage pipeline, with a person retained at two checkpoints by design rather than as a temporary limitation.

| Stage | Function | Implementation |
|-------|----------|----------------|
| 1 | Brief parsing — free text becomes structured fields | Gemini 2.5 Flash |
| 2 | Brand retrieval — only approved assets reach generation | ChromaDB |
| — | **Human checkpoint** — the parsed brief is reviewed before anything is generated | — |
| 3–5 | Generation — video drafted, brand-conditioned from the start | Google Flow |
| 6 | Resize, logo and overlay — one asset, sixteen social and web formats | FFmpeg, Pillow |
| 7 | Automated brand check — colour compliance, logo placement, unwanted text | OpenCV, Gemini |
| 8 | **Human sign-off** — nothing publishes unreviewed | Streamlit, SQLite |

Stages 3 to 5 are grouped because they run inside Google Flow, which exposes no public API. Generation is triggered manually and the completed file is picked up by a folder watcher, which is also what makes regeneration expensive — and therefore why the human checkpoint sits at stage 2, before any generation cost is incurred.

Every stage writes its own duration to a local database, so the evaluation data came out of the pipeline itself rather than from separate timing.

## Results

Multi-format resizing was the clearest gain — the task that previously consumed hours per asset now completes in seconds, and is no longer dependent on anyone's availability.

The more interesting result was the automated brand check, which passed a minority of outputs on first attempt. Over half of those failures traced to a single cause: text already present in the source product photography rather than generated by the model. That is a finding, not a failure — it locates precisely where the automation boundary sits, and it is why the human checkpoint is structural rather than provisional.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The conclusion the project turned on
Generating content was never the hard part. Keeping it on brand is — and that is where the human stays.
:::

## What I took from it

**Scoping a claim is as important as making it.** Early drafts of the review said "no study has measured AI against a manual baseline." One reviewed paper does exactly that, in a film production context. The defensible claim was narrower: no *included* study measured it against a documented manual baseline *in a retail content production context*. Learning to write claims that survive scrutiny changed how I write generally.

**Arithmetic has to reconcile.** Our exclusion counts summed to more than the number of papers excluded, because a paper could fail more than one criterion. Obvious once stated — but if a reader finds it before you explain it, every other number becomes suspect.

**Evidence and design are separate arguments.** A literature review that does not visibly change what gets built is decoration. The value came from the traceability: eight decisions, each with the finding that required it.
